We were supposed to reach Theth by six.

The more people hear about a quiet place, the less quiet it becomes.
The guesthouses are nowhere near as cheap as they were.
The valley sees far more walkers than it did.
The village is considerably more alive than it was.
So, Marcelo, you read my column. Be honest. Do we see eye to eye, or are you going to play devil's advocate?
A bit of both. You make a fair point about the money. The village is far more alive than it was. But the more people go there, the less special it feels.
That is a sweeping generalization, though. Some places are much better off with visitors than without them. Can you back that up?
I can. There is a beach I loved for years. The more hotels opened, the harder it was for local families to pay the rent. It is nowhere near as quiet as it was.
All right, I concede that one. But I still beg to differ on keeping places secret. A secret helps the people who already know it, not the people who live there.
Then I think we have to agree to disagree. Although, give me one more dinner and I might come around to your view.
That is a fair point, but I beg to differ.
The more people come, the less special it feels.
It is nowhere near as quiet as it was.
Can you back that up with an example?
I think we will have to agree to disagree.

Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. Thank you for reading the column before it went out. I have had far more emails about this one than about anything I have written this year, and they are nowhere near as polite as yours. About half of the readers think I am completely wrong. One man wrote that the more I write about quiet places, the faster they disappear, and honestly, that is a fair point. But very few people back up their opinion with anything real. So here is my plan. I am going to write a second column, and this time I would like to quote a real traveler who has seen a place change. You have been riding these roads for fifteen years. Would you be willing to give me two or three sentences? Call me when you can.

Here is something most of us were never taught. How to disagree without losing a friend. First, find the part you agree with, and say it out loud. That is a fair point. You have a point there. People relax when they hear it, and the more relaxed they are, the more they listen. Second, avoid sweeping generalizations. Words like always and never make an argument sound far stronger than it is, and much easier to attack. Third, back up your claim with one real example, not ten. One good story is worth more than a page of numbers. And finally, know when to stop. If the conversation is going nowhere, you can simply agree to disagree. The goal of a good argument is not to win. It is to leave the table still friends.

First, Fiona admits the problem: the more people hear about a quiet place, the less quiet it becomes. Then she gives the example of the valley above Theth, which now sees far more walkers than twenty years ago. After that, she plays devil's advocate and says the claim that tourism ruins places is a sweeping generalization. Next, she shows that the money from visitors has made the village considerably more alive. Finally, she refuses to sit on the fence and accepts that some readers will have to agree to disagree.
